about.title: I got here by taking things apart
paragraphs: Before it was C#, it was redstone contraptions in Minecraft. Same pleasure, smaller scale: watching something absurdly complex finally click. In 2022 I started writing add-ons and plugins for Minecraft Java, realised programming was exactly that feeling, and went looking for heavier languages. I landed on .NET in 2023 and never left.

Between 15 and 19 I worked freelance assembling dark poultry houses and swine facilities: feeders, nipple drinkers, curtains, emergency openings, misting systems, exhaust fans, plumbing, water tanks. Follow the manual, test the sensors, no duct tape, hand it over working. I may look like a skinny dev, but I know what it's like to be out in the field and have to solve it right there.

At RGO I started in IT support, because that was the opening. A year in, I could see how much of the company could be fixed with code, so I asked for the role change, and got it. Today I'm on the dev team: we review each other's code, decide architecture together, and nothing ships without every party signing off.

Outside of that: video games, board games, D&D, cooking something I've never made before, and an amount of coffee that would worry a doctor. I don't listen to music while I work; I end up listening to the music instead of working.

bullets: Full-stack internal applications in .NET, C# and Blazor, wired straight into the company's ERP so management sees one centralised view instead of six spreadsheets.
Custom reports and business-rule modules on top of ERP data, replacing manual routines.
Built the company's CI/CD pipelines from scratch in Azure DevOps; source control across Azure DevOps and GitHub.
Code review, architecture decisions and deploy validation for the automations each department builds.
Microsoft 365 and Active Directory: accounts, licences, permissions, mailboxes.
Infrastructure planning and support: workstations, equipment and network resources.
Rolled out business software with first- and second-level support.
Read technical drawings and assembled equipment for cattle, swine and poultry facilities.
Commissioned and tested installed systems against spec before handover.
Straight 100% across all three semesters so far.

projects.title: Things I built that people use
projects.lead: Problem, decision, result. Everything below runs in production at an industrial machinery manufacturer.

work.name: RgoSystem
work.problem: The ERP doesn't cover everything the company needs. What it doesn't cover turns into spreadsheets and undocumented workflows that live in someone's head.
work.decision: Blazor Server, because the backend is already C# and I wasn't giving up end-to-end type safety to write a web app. Direct data access through EF Core instead of standing up an API microservice for a system that is centralised anyway; mapped to the last millimetre.
work.result: One place for the company's automations, with the workflows documented instead of improvised. Over 60 people use it daily, and it has never gone down on me.

work.name: Protheus label printing
work.problem: Labels for incoming and internal materials were written by hand. The pen smudged, the label faded, and the shop floor lost track of what was what.
work.decision: Pull the data straight from the ERP and drive Zebra and Elesys printers from .NET, so a label is a consequence of the record, not a second, manual truth.
work.result: Labels come out printed, current, adhesive and legible. Receiving and internal shipping stopped guessing.

work.name: Microsoft 365 signature generator
work.problem: Email signatures were made by hand, one image at a time: heavy, inconsistent and outdated the moment someone changed roles.
work.decision: Generate them from the source of truth. Microsoft Graph already knows every user's data, so .NET renders the image from it.
work.result: 100% automated, standardised across the company, transparent, crisply rasterised, and under 20 KB each.

work.name: Azure delivery pipeline
work.problem: Applications were published by building to a folder and ClickOnce, tied to local infrastructure, with no repeatable path from commit to production.
work.decision: Put a new ASP.NET app on Azure and build the whole path properly: resource group, app service plan, Key Vault, virtual network, NAT gateway with a fixed outbound IP, custom domain, and GitHub Actions deploying per branch.
work.result: A commit to the right branch is a deploy. Nothing depends on a machine under someone's desk anymore.

music.title: Eight years of music
paragraphs: I joined the town's municipal band because my friends were there, and stayed because of the music: theory, classical repertoire, big arrangements. Today I play with the Banda Municipal de Serafina Corrêa and the city's orchestra, and the nights that stuck were the Teutônia music festivals in 2022 and 2025, huge arrangements played alongside hundreds of other young musicians.

Trombone is the one I actually have mastery in. But a mouthpiece is a mouthpiece, so hand me any brass instrument and something comes out of it; I play basic transverse flute, I'm studying violin, and I'll try whatever instrument happens to be within reach.
Nothing here makes a sound unless you ask it to. The game below is the only thing with audio, and it has a mute button.
No autoplay, no sound on this page. You're welcome.
